sessions.title: The power of micro-breaks
script: Hello. For the next four minutes, we'll talk about breaks. And then we'll take one, for real.
First, an idea that often surprises people: stress, in itself, isn't the problem.
Your body is built to rise to a challenge, then come back down. That's how it's meant to work.
What wears us down, many researchers say, is when the coming down never happens. When we go from effort to effort without ever recovering.
Picture a rubber band. If you stretch it and let it go often, it stays supple for years.
Keep it stretched all day, and it tires and loses its spring. Your nervous system is a little like that rubber band.
Many of us wait for the evening, or the weekend, to finally let go. By then, the fatigue has piled up.
Studies on work suggest that short, regular breaks, even a few minutes long, can help you keep your energy and limit fatigue through the day.
The good news: a micro-break is a skill you can learn. Let's take one now.
If you're in front of a screen, look away. Find the farthest point you can see: a window, the far end of the room.
Let your eyes rest there, without staring. Just looking far away.
Your eyes have been focusing up close for a long time. Now they can soften.
[pause 3s]
Now, your shoulders. Gently lift them up toward your ears as you breathe in.
And let them drop all at once as you breathe out through your mouth.
Feel the weight of your arms gently drawing your shoulders down.
One more time. Shoulders up… and down they fall, heavy.
Now the breath. Breathe in calmly through your nose, for a count of three or four.
Then breathe out more slowly, as if blowing on a spoonful of hot soup, with no hurry.
An out-breath longer than the in-breath is one of the simplest signals to help your body slow down.
Again. Breathe in through your nose… and let the air flow out slowly, all the way out.
And a third time, at your own pace. If you feel at all dizzy, just go back to your natural breathing.
Now, about thirty seconds of quiet, with just my voice to keep you company. Keep your eyes on that faraway point, or close them if you prefer.
[pause 4s]
There's nothing to do. Just be here. Feel the cool air coming in, and the slightly warmer air going out.
If a thought about work shows up, that's normal. Let it pass like a car going by, and come back to your breath.
[pause 4s]
Notice how you feel right now. Maybe a little more space. Maybe not much at all, and that's fine.
The effect of one micro-break is subtle. It's the repetition that makes the difference.
So for the rest of your day, a simple idea: scatter three micro-breaks through it.
One in the morning, maybe while your coffee is brewing, or just before you open your inbox.
One in the middle of the day, between two meetings, or on your way back from lunch.
And one in the late afternoon, before you leave work or move into your evening.
Each time, the same recipe, in under two minutes: look far away, drop your shoulders, lengthen your out-breath.
Tie each one to something you already do, like closing your laptop or getting a glass of water. That makes them easier to remember.
And here you are, back again. Wiggle your fingers, stretch if you like.
Remember the rubber band: you don't have to wait until tonight to let go. A few seconds, often, already go a long way.
sources: McEwen BS (1998). Protective and damaging effects of stress mediators. N Engl J Med 338:171-179 (allostatic load: harm comes from repeated/prolonged activation without recovery).
Meijman TF & Mulder G (1998). Psychological aspects of workload. In: Handbook of Work and Organizational Psychology (effort-recovery model).

Albulescu P et al. (2022). 'Give me a break!' A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance. PLOS ONE 17(8):e0272460 (micro-breaks associated with more vigor, less fatigue).
Sonnentag S & Fritz C (2015). Recovery from job stress: the stressor-detachment model. J Organ Behav 36:S72-S103.

Zaccaro A et al. (2018). How breath-control can change your life: a systematic review on psycho-physiological correlates of slow breathing. Front Hum Neurosci 12:353 (slow/long-exhale breathing and relaxation).

sessions.title: Coherent breathing
script: Here you are, for five minutes of coherent breathing: one of the best-known breathing practices, and one of the simplest.
The idea fits in one sentence: breathe slowly and steadily, about six times a minute. Five seconds in, five seconds out.
At this pace, for many people, heart and breath fall into step. The heart speeds up a little on the in-breath and slows on the out-breath, like a steady wave.
Studies suggest this slow breathing can help the body shift into recovery mode, and many people feel calmer doing it.
In France, it's often practiced as the "three-six-five" routine: three times a day, six breaths a minute, for five minutes.
On waking, before lunch, and in the late afternoon, when the day starts to weigh on you. Today, this counts as one of the three.
Sit upright, your back straight but not stiff, both feet flat on the floor.
Hands on your thighs, shoulders dropping. Close your eyes, or rest your gaze a little way ahead.
If you feel short of breath or light-headed, just go back to breathing naturally. Nothing to force.
Five seconds is only a guide. If it feels too long for you, shorten it a little: four seconds is perfectly fine too.
Let's begin. I'll count with you.
Breathe in slowly through your nose, let your belly rise… two… three… four… five.
And breathe out gently, through your nose or your mouth… two… three… four… five.
Breathe in again, effortlessly… two… three… four… five.
Breathe out, your shoulders softening… two… three… four… five.
Breathe in, like a wave rolling up the sand… two… three… four… five.
Breathe out, the wave slipping slowly back… two… three… four… five.
Breathe in… your belly gently rounding… three… four… five.
Breathe out… your belly settling back down… three… four… five.
Breathe in, not filling up, just enough… four… five.
Breathe out, not pushing, just letting go… four… five.
One minute. Breathe in, keeping that same steady rhythm.
Breathe out, just as slowly, no rush.
Breathe in, and feel the cool air at the tip of your nose.
Breathe out, and feel the slightly warmer air leaving.
Breathe in… your heart speeds up ever so slightly.
Breathe out… and it slows again, all by itself.
Breathe in, gently filling a balloon in your belly.
Breathe out, the balloon slowly empties.
Breathe in… four… five.
Breathe out… four… five.
Breathe in, nothing to do but breathe.
Breathe out, and let your hands grow heavy on your thighs.
If your mind wanders off to your to-do list, no problem at all. Just come back with the next breath in.
Two minutes. Breathe in, around five seconds.
Breathe out. If your mind drifts, just come back to the breath.
Breathe in, the wave rises.
Breathe out, the wave falls back.
Breathe in, letting your chest and your belly open together.
Breathe out, as softly as a sigh that takes its time.
Breathe in… three… four… five.
Breathe out… three… four… five.
Breathe in, your jaw loosening, your forehead smoothing out.
Breathe out, your body sinking into the chair.
Breathe in, steady as a calm metronome.
Breathe out, always at the same speed, smooth and even.
Three minutes. Breathe in, you're past the halfway point now.
Breathe out, and notice this rhythm settling in you.
Breathe in, as if the breath came on its own.
Breathe out, and let it go again, without holding on.
Breathe in, and feel your feet resting on the floor.
Breathe out, and feel your back supported.
Breathe in, breathing for yourself, just for you.
Breathe out, the day can wait a little longer.
Four minutes. For this last one, I'll stay quieter. Keep the rhythm in your own way.
Breathe in… slowly… your belly rising…
[pause 3s]
And breathe out… slowly… everything settling…
Breathe in again… cool air… all the way down to your belly…
[pause 3s]
Breathe out, very gently… like a long sigh…
One last time, breathe in… three… four… five.
And breathe out, long and slow… four… five… all the way out.
[pause 3s]
Now let your breathing return to its natural rhythm.
[pause 3s]
Notice how your body feels. Warmth in your hands, maybe. The weight of your shoulders. The rhythm of your heart.
There's nothing you need to feel. Just notice how you are, right now.
Gently move your fingers, and open your eyes if they were closed.
This rhythm is part of you now. You can come back to it wherever you are: on the train, at your desk, before you fall asleep. Five minutes, three times a day, if it does you good.
sources: Lehrer PM & Gevirtz R (2014). Heart rate variability biofeedback: how and why does it work? Front Psychol 5:756 (resonance breathing around 6 breaths/min, ~0.1 Hz; individual resonance frequency varies roughly 4.5-7/min).
Laborde S et al. (2022). Effects of voluntary slow breathing on heart rate and heart rate variability: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Neurosci Biobehav Rev 138:104711.
Zaccaro A et al. (2018). Front Hum Neurosci 12:353 (slow breathing, relaxation, autonomic effects).
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia: heart rate rises on inhalation and falls on exhalation (standard physiology; e.g. Yasuma & Hayano 2004, Chest 125:683-690).

'365' schedule (3x/day, 6 breaths/min, 5 min): popularised in France by Dr David O'Hare (Cohérence cardiaque 365, 2012). The specific 3x/day schedule is a practical convention, not a validated dose - wording kept as 'on la propose souvent'.

sessions.title: Stress as an ally?
script: Welcome. Today, a slightly unexpected question: what if your stress were trying to help you?
Get comfortable, sitting or standing, whatever suits you. Take one breath a little deeper than the others.
When you face a challenge, your body gears up. Your heart beats faster, your breathing speeds up. Sometimes you feel heat, or butterflies in your stomach.
We've learned to see these signs as a threat, as proof that something is wrong.
Yet this reaction has a very concrete job: it sends more energy and oxygen to your muscles and your brain. Your body is getting ready to act.
It's a bit like warming up a car on a winter morning. The engine runs louder, but only so that you can get moving.
Researchers, especially in the United States, have studied what changes when we look at this reaction differently.
In several experiments, people about to face a stressful test, like giving a talk or sitting an exam, were told that their pounding heart was a resource, fuel for the task.
These people often felt more confident. And in some of them, the heart and blood vessels responded more like they do for a challenge than for a threat.

Another study tested one simple sentence, said just before singing or speaking in public: "I am excited." People who said it seemed a little more at ease than those who tried telling themselves "I am calm."
Why? Perhaps because it's very hard to jump straight from agitation to calm. It's much easier to change the name we give that agitation.
Other research suggests that seeing stress as something that can also help us grow is linked to handling it more calmly day to day.

Careful, though: this doesn't mean all stress is good, or that you should put up with everything in silence. Stress that's too intense, or that lasts for months, deserves to be taken seriously, sometimes with the help of a professional.
The idea is simpler: in the face of a one-off challenge, what you tell yourself about your sensations can change how you move through them.
We're not trying to calm down at all costs. We're trying to turn "I'm panicking" into "I'm getting ready."
Let's try it together.
Think of something coming up that stresses you a little. Not the worst thing in your life: something moderate, manageable.
An important appointment, a meeting where you have to speak, a conversation you keep putting off, an exam.
Choose one, and imagine you're there. The place, the people, the moment just before it begins.
[pause 3s]
Now turn your attention to your body. No need to change anything, just observe.
Your heart, first. Is it beating a little faster, a little harder? Maybe you can feel it in your chest, or your throat.
Your breath. Is it shorter, higher up in your chest?
Maybe you also feel like moving, tapping your foot, getting up. That's energy looking for a direction.
And heat. In your face, your hands, your belly. Maybe a slight restlessness in your legs, or a knot in your stomach.
Whatever you notice is normal. It's your body responding to something that matters to you.

You may notice these are almost the same sensations as excitement, before a concert or a first date. Your body doesn't always know the difference. Often, it's the interpretation that changes everything.
[pause 3s]
Now let's look at these same sensations differently. One at a time.
Your racing heart: it's sending more blood to your muscles and your brain. You can say to yourself, silently: "My body is giving me energy."
Your quickening breath: it's bringing in more oxygen. Tell yourself: "I'm breathing to get ready."
The heat, the butterflies: they're a sign that this situation matters to you. You wouldn't feel this way about something meaningless.
And now, try this sentence, slowly: "My body is getting ready."
[pause 3s]
"My body is getting ready. It's on my side."
[pause 3s]
Notice whether anything shifts, even slightly. The sensations may still be there, but they don't feel quite the same.
And if nothing changes, that's fine. This is training, and it grows stronger with repetition.
Think of a musician just before going on stage. They often still get nervous, even after years of performing. They don't wait for the nerves to disappear before they play: they play with them.
To support this new view, let's give your body a posture of momentum rather than retreat.
Gently straighten your back. Let your chest open, your shoulders widen a little toward the back. Your head is upright, your chin level with the floor.
Place your feet flat, as if you were putting down roots.
And now, a steady breath. Not necessarily slow, just even.
Breathe in through your nose, for a count of four… one… two… three… four.
And breathe out, for five or six, without forcing… two… three… four… five… six.
[pause 3s]
You keep the energy, but you give it a direction. Like an athlete on the starting line: focused, awake, ready to go.
One more breath. Breathe in… two… three… four.
And breathe out, smoothly… three… four… five… six. If you feel at all dizzy, simply go back to your natural breathing.
Picture yourself in the situation again. This time, with that straight back, that steady breath, and that sentence in mind.
Your heart may still be beating fast, and that's perfectly fine: it's working for you.
See yourself begin, say your first words, make your first move. Not perfectly. Simply there, with your energy.
You can feel your heart beating fast, and at the same time feel your feet on the floor and your steady breath. Both can be there together.
[pause 4s]
Let the image fade. Come back to the room you're in, to the feeling of your feet on the floor.
Notice how you feel about that situation now. A little more drive, perhaps. Or simply a little more clarity.

Here's what I'd like you to take with you. When the moment comes and you feel your heart speed up, just before you walk in, pick up the phone or start speaking, plant your feet, stand tall, and say it again: "My body is getting ready."
You don't need to make stress disappear to move forward. You can bring it with you, as an ally.
sources: Jamieson JP, Nock MK & Mendes WB (2012). Mind over matter: reappraising arousal improves cardiovascular and cognitive responses to stress. J Exp Psychol Gen 141(3):417-422 (reappraisal before a social stress test -> more 'challenge-like' cardiovascular profile).
Jamieson JP et al. (2010). Turning the knots in your stomach into bows: reappraising arousal improves performance on the GRE. J Exp Soc Psychol 46:208-212.
Crum AJ, Salovey P & Achor S (2013). Rethinking stress: the role of mindsets in determining the stress response. J Pers Soc Psychol 104(4):716-733 (stress-is-enhancing mindset).
Brooks AW (2014). Get excited: reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement. J Exp Psychol Gen 143(3):1144-1158.
Blascovich J & Mendes WB (2000/2010): challenge vs threat cardiovascular patterns (biopsychosocial model).
Note: effects are modest and context-dependent; script states it does not apply to chronic/overwhelming stress and suggests professional help.

sessions.title: The negativity bias
script: Hello. Take a moment to arrive here. Let your body find a position where it can settle.
You can sit, lie down, or even stay standing. What matters is being comfortable for the next few minutes.
Think about yesterday. What comes back to you first?
Chances are it's an annoyance: a sharp word, a delay, an irritating email.
And yet that same day surely held some pleasant moments. A hot coffee, a smile, a ray of sunshine.
Or think of one criticism among ten compliments. Which one do you replay at night while brushing your teeth?
Or this one: on a drive, a hundred polite drivers pass you, and one cuts you off. Guess which one you talk about when you get home.
That's no accident. Psychologists call it the negativity bias: for the same intensity, a negative event usually leaves a stronger mark than a positive one.
An American psychologist summed it up with an image: for bad experiences, our brain is like Velcro, they stick right away. For good ones, it's more like Teflon, they slide off.
This isn't a flaw in your character. It's an inheritance.
For our ancestors, missing a sweet fruit wasn't a big deal. Missing a predator could cost them their life.
Brains that spotted danger quickly, and remembered it, had a survival advantage.

Today there's no predator in the hallway. But the brain keeps scanning for threats, and that can feed a constant background hum of stress. In a way, it behaves like a news channel that mostly reports the bad news.
The good news is that we can tip the balance back a little.
Research on what's called savoring suggests that taking time to linger on good moments is linked to more positive emotions.
Savoring is what you naturally do with a delicious dessert: you slow down and make each bite last. You can do the same with a moment in your day.
The idea is simple: a pleasant moment doesn't sink in on its own. But if you stay with it for a few dozen seconds, feeling it in your body, it probably has a better chance of leaving a trace.
We're not denying difficulties, or looking at life through rose-tinted glasses. We're simply giving good moments time to exist.
Let's do it now.
Close your eyes if you'd like. Take two easy breaths.
Let your belly rise as you breathe in, and settle as you breathe out.
[pause 3s]
Look for a small, pleasant moment from the last few days. Not a big event: something simple.
The first sip of coffee. A conversation that made you laugh. Cool, fresh sheets. Sun on your face as you stepped outside. A kind message.
Take the first one that comes. It doesn't have to be perfect.
And if nothing comes, that's fine. You can choose something present: the warmth of your hands, the comfort of your seat, the simple fact of taking this time for yourself.
Now relive this moment in detail, as if you were there again.
Where are you? What do you see around you? The colors, the light, the shapes. Who's there with you, if anyone?
[pause 3s]
What do you hear? A voice, music, silence, the sound of the street.
Is there a smell, a taste? A temperature, a texture against your skin? Take your time with each detail. There's no rush.
And what were you feeling in that moment? Joy, ease, tenderness, lightness?
Let that feeling come back, even just a little. It doesn't need to be as strong as on the day itself.
Now we'll stretch this moment out. Stay with it, without moving on. Just for twenty seconds or so.
Find where it lives in your body. Warmth in your chest, perhaps. A smile at the corner of your mouth. Softer shoulders.
There's no right way to feel it. A little warmth, a slight smile, a bit more space: it all counts.
[pause 4s]
If your mind wanders off to a task or a worry, that's normal: that's the Velcro doing its job. Gently come back to your moment.
[pause 3s]
Let the feeling spread, like a patch of light slowly widening inside you.
Breathe in, welcoming this moment… and breathe out, letting it settle into you.
If it feels good, let it grow a little. Breathe with it. With each in-breath, imagine it taking up a bit more space.
Now imagine this moment sinking into you. Like water slowly soaking into a sponge. Or like warmth spreading out from the center of your chest.
There's nothing to force. You simply let this good experience in, and let it find its place.
Some people like to imagine placing the moment in a treasured box inside them, where they can come back for it on grayer days.
[pause 4s]
You can say to yourself, silently: "This is part of my life too."
[pause 3s]
Notice how that sentence lands in your body. Does it ring true, or feel a little strange? Both are welcome.
Now let the image drift away, keeping whatever remains of it in your body.
Notice how you feel. Maybe a little softer. Maybe nothing dramatic, and that's fine. Like a muscle, this ability builds little by little.
Savoring doesn't mean hard moments don't count. They do. But they aren't the whole story.
Here's the practice I'd suggest: three times a day, when a small pleasant moment comes along, pause.
The taste of your lunch, the light at the end of the day, a loved one's voice on the phone.
Even something as small as warm water on your hands, or the smell of bread as you walk past a bakery.
Instead of rushing on to the next thing, stay with it for about twenty seconds. Feel it in your body. Let it sink in. Twenty seconds is roughly three or four slow breaths.
It takes almost no time. But day after day, you're teaching your brain to notice what's going well, too. You may find these moments start catching your attention more easily, almost on their own.
You can also do it at night, once you're in bed: recall three good moments from your day and linger on each one, instead of replaying what went wrong.
Come back gently. Take a slightly deeper breath, move your hands, and open your eyes whenever it feels right.
sources: Baumeister RF et al. (2001). Bad is stronger than good. Rev Gen Psychol 5(4):323-370.
Rozin P & Royzman EB (2001). Negativity bias, negativity dominance, and contagion. Pers Soc Psychol Rev 5(4):296-320.

Hanson R (2013). Hardwiring Happiness (velcro/teflon metaphor; 'taking in the good', staying 10-30 s with a positive experience). Hanson R et al. (2023). Learning to learn from positive experiences. J Posit Psychol 18(1):142-153 (preliminary evidence for the HEAL programme).

Bryant FB & Veroff J (2007). Savoring: A New Model of Positive Experience. Erlbaum. Smith JL & Bryant FB (2017). The benefits of savoring life: savoring as a moderator of the relationship between health and life satisfaction / savoring interventions review, Int J Aging Hum Dev 84(1):3-23.

Evolutionary explanation of negativity bias = mainstream hypothesis (Rozin & Royzman 2001; Vaish, Grossmann & Woodward 2008, Psychol Bull 134:383-403). The '20 s helps memory encoding' idea is framed cautiously ('sans doute plus de chances').

sessions.title: Your cortisol rhythm
script: This session works best at the end of the day. If you're listening at another time, the practice will help you prepare your evening ritual.
Get comfortable, and let your breath settle.
Cortisol has a bad reputation. It's often called the stress hormone, as if we should get rid of it.
Some people even think of it as an enemy, something to fight or to keep as low as possible all day long.
In fact, your body needs it every day. It helps mobilize energy, regulate blood sugar, wake you up and meet challenges.
Above all, it follows a rhythm, set by your internal clock: a small region deep in the brain that keeps time over roughly twenty-four hours.
This rhythm is like a tide. Cortisol starts to rise in the second half of the night, to prepare you for waking.
Then, within about half an hour of waking up, it reaches a peak. Researchers call this the cortisol awakening response. It's a bit like a boost to help you start the day.
After that, as the hours go by, the tide slowly goes out. In the evening, levels are low, and they reach their lowest point early in the night. That dip makes room for sleep.

Think of the light on a summer day: it rises in the morning, shines at noon, then slowly fades into evening. Your cortisol curve looks a little like that, except that it gets up a little before you do.
High in the morning, low at night: that's the usual pattern for most people.

Cortisol doesn't work alone. In the evening, as it falls and the light fades, another hormone takes over: melatonin, which tells your body it's nighttime. The two respond to each other, a little like dance partners.
This rhythm also varies from person to person. Some people are morning types, others are night owls. The point isn't to fit a mold, but to find a regular rhythm that suits you.
What can throw this tide off is often our modern way of life.
Bright light late in the evening, from screens and ceiling lights, can tell your clock it's still daytime.
Your clock can't read the time on your phone. It mostly reads light, and bright light says daytime.
Stress that drags on into the evening, emails at ten at night, tense conversations before bed, keeps your body in action mode.
And very irregular hours, going to bed and getting up at very different times from one day to the next, blur your clock's signals.

Studies have also observed that in people under stress for a long time, this curve tends to flatten: less difference between morning and evening, less get-up-and-go on waking, more trouble switching off at night.
On the other hand, a few simple habits help the clock keep time.
Morning light, first. Spending a few minutes outside, or sitting near a window soon after you get up, is one of the strongest signals for setting your internal clock.
Even on a gray day, outdoor light is far brighter than a lit room.
Breaks during the day, too, so you're not tense from morning to night.
And in the evening, slowing down: dimming the lights, setting screens aside a little before bed, and signaling to your body that the day is over.
In the evening, soft, low light, like a bedside lamp, is a simple way of telling your clock that the day is coming to an end.
Screens aren't forbidden. The idea is mainly to avoid staying under bright light, with content that winds you up, until the very last minute.
None of this is a strict rule. These are invitations to go with your rhythm rather than against it.
Let's practice this evening slow-down now.
If you can, dim the lights around you. Switch off the overhead light, keep a small lamp on. If you can't move, simply imagine the room gently growing darker.
[pause 3s]
You can also turn down your screen's brightness, or place your phone face down. If you like, tuck your feet under a blanket, and notice the temperature of the room.
Now slow your movements. If you move your hands, do it twice as slowly as usual. As if you were moving through water.
Try it, if you like: slowly raise one hand, as if it were floating, then lower it, in slow motion. This simple slowness tells your body there's no rush.
Rest your hands on your thighs, or on your belly. Feel their weight.
[pause 3s]
Your face can slow down too. Your forehead smooths out. Your eyelids grow heavy. Your jaw loosens.
Your arms grow heavy. Your hands settle. Even your thoughts can slow down, like a conversation winding down at the end of a meal.
Now let's lengthen the out-breath. It's a simple way to help your body shift into recovery mode.
Breathe in through your nose, calmly, for a count of four… one… two… three… four.
And breathe out slowly, for a count of six, as if to make a candle flame flicker without blowing it out… two… three… four… five… six.
Once more. Breathe in, without forcing… two… three… four.
And let the air flow out, long and slow, all the way out… three… four… five… six.
A third time, at your own pace. Breathe in… your belly rises… and breathe out… your shoulders drop… your face softens.
Carry on at your own pace. With each out-breath, imagine the tide going out inside you. The day's tasks recede, like water leaving the sand smooth behind it.
If you feel any discomfort, go back to your natural breathing.

Now imagine your body is a house where the lights go off, room by room. The office light goes off: work thoughts fall quiet. Then the kitchen: the lists, the shopping, the things to plan. All that's left is one small lamp, soft and warm.
[pause 4s]
Notice the signs that your body is shifting into evening mode. Lower shoulders. A small yawn, maybe. Warmth in your hands or feet. A wish to slow down even more.
There's nothing to achieve. Your body knows how to make this transition. You're simply giving it the right conditions.
[pause 3s]
Feel the day behind you. Whatever isn't finished can wait until tomorrow. Tonight, there's nothing left to solve.
[pause 3s]
Before we finish, let's choose two small habits together. One for the morning, one for the evening.
For the morning, for example: opening the curtains as soon as you get up, drinking your coffee by the window, or walking outside for a few minutes before your day begins.
Choose the one that feels easiest. The smallest habit is often the one that lasts.
[pause 3s]
For the evening: dimming the lights at the same time every night, leaving your phone in another room, or repeating these long out-breaths before bed.
Choose one here, too.
[pause 3s]
Bright mornings, dim evenings: two simple habits to support your inner tide.
If sleep problems or tiredness have been going on for a long time, don't hesitate to talk to a health professional.
For now, keep this slowness with you. And if you're heading to bed, keep the lights low on the way.
sources: Stalder T et al. (2016). Assessment of the cortisol awakening response: expert consensus guidelines. Psychoneuroendocrinology 63:414-432 (CAR peaks ~30-45 min after waking).
Fries E, Dettenborn L & Kirschbaum C (2009). The cortisol awakening response (CAR): facts and future directions. Int J Psychophysiol 72:67-73.

Diurnal cortisol rhythm: rise in the second half of the night, nadir around the beginning of the night/midnight (e.g. Weitzman ED et al. 1971, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 33:14-22; Chan S & Debono M 2010, Ther Adv Endocrinol Metab 1(3):129-138).
Suprachiasmatic nucleus as master clock; light is the main zeitgeber (e.g. Czeisler CA et al. 1989, Science 244:1328-1333; Blume C, Garbazza C & Spitschan M 2019, Somnologie 23:147-156).
Gooley JJ et al. (2011). Exposure to room light before bedtime suppresses melatonin onset and shortens melatonin duration in humans. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 96(3):E463-E472.
Irregular schedules / circadian misalignment: Scheer FAJL et al. (2009) PNAS 106:4453-4458; Phillips AJK et al. (2017) Sci Rep 7:3216 (sleep regularity).
Script makes no claim that light or practices 'lower' cortisol; morning light described as helping set the internal clock.

Adam EK et al. (2017). Diurnal cortisol slopes and mental and physical health outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychoneuroendocrinology 83:25-41 (flatter slopes associated with chronic stress and poorer outcomes; observational).
Melatonin rises in the evening under dim light (Gooley 2011 above); chronotypes vary between individuals (Roenneberg T et al. 2007, Sleep Med Rev 11:429-438).

sessions.title: What stress does in your body
script: Welcome to this exploration of stress. Over the next eight minutes, you'll understand what happens in your body when stress rises, and then learn how to press the brake.
Settle in however you like. No need to close your eyes yet, just listen.
Picture a smoke detector. It's there to protect you. When it senses danger, it goes off loudly, and that's exactly what we want it to do.
Your brain has an alarm system that works in much the same way. It's very old: we share it with many animals. It helped our ancestors escape predators.

At the heart of this alarm is a small, almond-shaped area called the amygdala, which picks up anything that looks like a threat. It acts very fast, often before you've had time to think. That's why you can jump before you even understand what's happening.
Think of slamming on the brakes to avoid a cyclist: in a split second, before you've even thought about it, your body has already reacted.

The trouble is that today, this detector often goes off over a slightly burnt piece of toast. A full inbox, a traffic jam, a comment from a coworker. No real danger to your life, but the alarm sounds anyway.
Your body doesn't always tell the difference between a lion and a presentation in front of your boss: in both cases, it gets roughly the same resources ready.
It's a bit as if your phone sounded the same siren for a text from a friend and for a fire alarm.
When the alarm sounds, two things happen, as if someone pressed the accelerator.

First, within seconds, your body releases adrenaline. That's what makes your heart beat faster, speeds up your breathing, tenses your muscles, and sometimes gives you sweaty palms or a knot in your stomach.
Meanwhile, anything that isn't urgent takes a back seat. Digestion slows down, for example. Your body puts its resources into action.
Then, a little more slowly, over several minutes, a second pathway takes over: a chain linking the brain to small glands sitting on top of the kidneys, which releases cortisol.
Cortisol mobilizes energy, in particular by raising the sugar available in your blood. It helps your body keep going.
Picture a runner on the starting line: heart pounding, muscles ready, energy available. That's exactly what adrenaline and cortisol are preparing you for.
All of this is useful, in the short term. It's what lets you react, focus, and push yourself.

But an accelerator isn't enough. Your body also has a brake: the recovery system. It slows the heart, relaxes the muscles, gets digestion going again. It tells your body: it's over, you can rest. Scientists call it the parasympathetic nervous system, but you can simply call it the brake.

Normally, after the alarm, the brake takes over. The problem is when the accelerator stays pressed down, day after day. Studies link this kind of prolonged stress with fatigue, poorer sleep, and other effects on health.
The good news is that you can partly press this brake yourself. And one of the most accessible ways is your breath, especially the out-breath.
Before pressing the brake, let's learn to notice when the accelerator is down.
If you like, close your eyes, or simply lower your gaze.
Take a natural breath, and begin to scan your body, like a kind detective. You're not trying to change anything, just observing.
You can start at the top of your body and slowly work your way down, one area at a time.
Start with your jaw. Is it clenched? Are your teeth touching?
[pause 2s]
Your forehead, around your eyes. Is there a frown, any tightness?
Your shoulders. Are they hunched up toward your ears, or low and resting?
[pause 2s]
Your breathing. Is it high in your chest, and quick? Or slow, and deep in your belly?
Rest a hand on your belly if you like, to feel where your breath is sitting.
Your heart. Can you feel it beating? Fast, or calm?
No need to take your pulse. Just notice what you can sense, and what you can't.
Your belly. Is it knotted, tight, or soft?
[pause 2s]
Your hands. Are they clenched, sweaty, cold, or relaxed?
Whatever you find is useful information. There's nothing to fix right now.
Simply note what you find, like ticking off a list. Jaw clenched, yes or no. Shoulders up, yes or no. Nothing more.
[pause 3s]
Maybe you found a few signs of the accelerator. Maybe very few. Either way, you've just done something important: checked in with your body.
Now let's press the brake.
Breathe in gently through your nose, without filling your lungs completely… two… three.
And breathe out slowly through your mouth, as if blowing through a straw. Longer than the in-breath… four… five… six.
[pause 3s]
As you breathe out, your heart naturally tends to slow down a little. It's a normal mechanism, and you can use it to your advantage.
Once more. Breathe in through your nose… two… three.
And breathe out, long and slow… four… five… six. Let your shoulders drop with the air flowing out.
[pause 3s]

Carry on like this, at your own pace. A simple in-breath, a longer out-breath. You can count in your head: three or four to breathe in, six to breathe out. If you feel light-headed, go back to your usual breathing.
With each out-breath, release one of the areas you noticed earlier. Your jaw, first. Let a little space open between your teeth.
Breathe in… and as the air slowly leaves, let your tongue relax in your mouth too.
[pause 3s]
Then your forehead. It smooths out, like a sheet being shaken flat. Your shoulders settle a little lower.
Your hands open and rest, palms up if that's comfortable. Your belly can soften, and move freely with the breath.
Breathe in again… and breathe out slowly. Your breath becomes the foot resting gently on the brake pedal.
Imagine the smoke detector falling silent. The toast is out of the toaster, the window is open, and the air is clear again.
[pause 3s]
Now let your breathing return to normal. And quickly scan again: jaw, shoulders, breath, heart, belly, hands.
What has changed? Maybe a little more heaviness, warmth, space. Maybe the change is tiny. That's fine: your brake is training, like a muscle.
[pause 2s]
Here's something to explore next. Everyone has their own warning signals. For some, it's a clenched jaw. For others, a knotted stomach, a held breath, or shoulders creeping up.
Over the next few days, try to spot yours. The very first sign that shows up when the alarm goes off.
It might help to think back to the last time you felt stressed. What did your body do first?
The day you recognize it, you'll know the accelerator is down. And you'll know what to do: one long out-breath, and one area that lets go.
The earlier you spot it, the easier it is to brake. A bit like driving: easing off gently before a bend takes far less effort than slamming on the brakes at the last moment.
If these signals are very frequent, very intense, or get in the way of daily life, talk to a doctor or a psychologist. That's what they're there for.
Gently open your eyes. You now know your alarm, your accelerator, and your brake.
sources: Sapolsky RM (2004). Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers, 3rd ed. Holt (alarm system, acute vs chronic stress; zebra/predator framing).
McEwen BS (1998). N Engl J Med 338:171-179; McEwen BS (2007). Physiology and neurobiology of stress and adaptation. Physiol Rev 87:873-904 (chronic activation and health).

Ulrich-Lai YM & Herman JP (2009). Neural regulation of endocrine and autonomic stress responses. Nat Rev Neurosci 10:397-409 (fast sympathetic-adrenomedullary response in seconds; slower HPA axis -> cortisol over minutes).
Dickerson SS & Kemeny ME (2004). Acute stressors and cortisol responses: a theoretical integration and synthesis. Psychol Bull 130(3):355-391 (cortisol peaks ~20-40 min after stressor onset).
Smoke detector analogy: Nesse RM (2005). Natural selection and the regulation of defenses: a signal detection analysis of the smoke detector principle. Evol Hum Behav 26:88-105.
Exhale-related heart slowing (respiratory sinus arrhythmia): Yasuma F & Hayano J (2004). Chest 125:683-690. Chronic stress & sleep: Kim EJ & Dimsdale JE (2007) Behav Sleep Med 5:256-278.

LeDoux JE (2000). Emotion circuits in the brain. Annu Rev Neurosci 23:155-184 (amygdala, rapid threat detection before conscious appraisal). Note: 'amygdale cérébrale' used in FR to avoid confusion with tonsils.

sessions.title: Stress and connection
script: If you can, settle near something warm. A blanket, a mug, a soft lamp. Take your time to arrive.
Let your breath settle. Feel the places where your body is supported, whatever is holding you right now.
Breathe in calmly… and breathe out, letting your shoulders grow a little heavier. Once more, at your own pace.
[pause 3s]
When we talk about stress, we usually think of two reactions: fight or flight. A racing heart, muscles ready to spring.
In the year two thousand, an American researcher, Shelley Taylor, and her team suggested adding to that picture.
The team noticed that, under stress, many humans also do something else: they move closer to others. They take care of the most vulnerable, and they seek support.
The researchers called this "tend and befriend": caring for others, and reaching out.
Think about what happens after bad news. Often, the first reflex is to call someone, to check on the people we love, to hold our children close. That's exactly it.
Or think of those stormy nights when neighbors who barely say hello suddenly find themselves in the hallway, helping each other out.
Several hormones seem to be involved in this urge to connect, and researchers are still exploring their exact role.
Shelley Taylor's work focused mainly on women. But other teams have observed that, under stress, men also became more cooperative and generous. This tendency seems to exist in all of us.
And it's more than a nice idea. Connection with others is one of the strongest buffers against stress.
You can think of it as a cushion between you and the hard knocks of life.
In one study, for example, people had to speak in front of a panel. Those who had spent time with a friend just beforehand showed a smaller stress response in their bodies.

Large health studies also show that people with good social ties are, on average, in better health. What matters isn't necessarily how many friends you have, but the feeling that you can count on someone. Studies even suggest that brief, friendly exchanges, with a neighbor or the person at the bakery, can lift our mood.
So when stress rises and you feel like calling someone, that's not weakness. It's your body reaching for a very old, and often very effective, resource.
And connection works both ways. For many people, offering support seems to do good to the giver as well.
Let's explore this together now.
Close your eyes if that's comfortable. Breathe easily.
Breathe in through your nose… and let the out-breath last a little longer. Your body settles.
Imagine yourself somewhere you feel good. A cozy room, a garden, a corner of the sofa.
Now think of someone who supports you. Someone you feel safe with, someone you can be yourself around.
It might be a friend, a family member, a coworker, a neighbor. It might also be someone you haven't seen in a long time, a teacher who believed in you, or even a pet you love.
Choose whoever comes most easily. There's no wrong answer here.
Imagine this person near you. Their face, their smile, the way they look at you. Notice the small details: the color of a sweater, a familiar gesture, the sound of their laugh.
[pause 3s]
Then let a second person come to mind. And maybe a third. They take their places around you, in a circle.
If only a few faces come, that's completely normal. One person is enough. You can also include someone who helped you once, even briefly.
Look at each of these people, one after the other. Remember a specific moment when they were there for you. A piece of advice, a fit of laughter, a quiet presence.
Hear their voice, perhaps. Something they once said to you that did you good.
[pause 3s]
Feel their presence. They're not asking anything of you. They're simply here, on your side. Let yourself enjoy this, even for a few seconds.
Notice what happens in your body as you imagine them around you. Warmth in your chest, maybe. Shoulders softening. Your breath deepening.
Many people feel their body relax just by thinking of someone kind. Simply let yourself taste that feeling.
[pause 3s]
Imagine one of them placing a hand on your shoulder. A warm, reassuring hand. As if to say: I'm here, with you.
If you like, actually rest your own hand on your shoulder, or on your arm. Your body understands this language too.
Let that warmth spread, from your shoulder into your back, then into your chest.
Breathe in slowly… and as you breathe out, let your chest soften into that warmth.
[pause 3s]
If something difficult is weighing on you right now, imagine setting it down in the middle of the circle. You're no longer the only one carrying it. Other eyes are looking at it with you.
You don't have to solve it right now. Just feel that it's a little lighter when it's shared.
[pause 3s]
Now, let's turn things around.
Think of someone you could support today. Someone going through a hard time, facing a stressful moment, or who seems a little isolated lately.
Picture them in front of you. And silently send them a few simple words: I'm thinking of you. I hope you're okay. I'm here.
You don't need to have solutions for them. Often, what helps most is simply feeling seen, and heard.
[pause 3s]
Notice what it does inside you to offer them this attention. Caring for someone often calms us too.
Perhaps a smile, a softness, a quiet sense of pride. Let that feeling settle in over a few breaths.
[pause 2s]
Now let's turn this moment into something concrete.
Of all the people who came to mind, choose one to contact, today or tomorrow. Someone who supports you, or someone you could support.
And choose how: a simple message, a five-minute call, an invitation for coffee, a walk.
No need for a big conversation, or a perfect one. A quick "I was thinking of you" is often enough to bring two people closer.
For example: "I thought of you this morning, how are you doing?" Or: "Fancy a coffee this week?"
And if you're hesitating, afraid of bothering them, studies suggest we often underestimate how much an unexpected little message is appreciated. Most people are touched to be thought of.
You can even decide, silently, when you'll do it. Tonight after dinner. Tomorrow on your break.
See yourself doing it. Your phone in your hand, the first words you type. And the reply, perhaps, arriving with a smile.
Notice how simple it really is. A few seconds for you, and maybe a bright spot in someone else's day.
Notice how you feel now, after this time spent in good company. Maybe a little warmer, a little lighter in the shoulders.
Now let the circle gently fade, keeping its warmth with you. These bonds exist, even when people are far away.
Come back to the feeling of your body, your breath, the sounds around you.
And if you're going through a time when loneliness weighs heavily, remember you can also turn to a doctor, a therapist, or a support line. Asking for help is another way of creating connection.
Open your eyes whenever you like. And don't forget your message: someone, somewhere, may be very happy to receive it.
sources: Taylor SE et al. (2000). Biobehavioral responses to stress in females: tend-and-befriend, not fight-or-flight. Psychol Rev 107(3):411-429 (proposed mainly for females; later work extends it more broadly).
Cohen S & Wills TA (1985). Stress, social support, and the buffering hypothesis. Psychol Bull 98(2):310-357.

Heinrichs M et al. (2003). Social support and oxytocin interact to suppress cortisol and subjective responses to psychosocial stress. Biol Psychiatry 54:1389-1398 (support from a friend before the TSST attenuated cortisol response).
Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB & Layton JB (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review. PLoS Med 7(7):e1000316 (perceived/functional support matters, not only network size).

Inagaki TK & Eisenberger NI (2016). Giving support to others reduces sympathetic nervous system-related responses to stress. Psychophysiology 53:427-435; Brown SL et al. (2003). Psychol Sci 14:320-327 (giving support associated with health benefits).
von Dawans B et al. (2012). The social dimension of stress reactivity: acute stress increases prosocial behavior in humans. Psychol Sci 23:651-660 (men too).
Liu PJ, Rim S, Min L & Min KE (2023). The surprise of reaching out: appreciated more than we think. J Pers Soc Psychol 124(4):754-771.
Sandstrom GM & Dunn EW (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Pers Soc Psychol Bull 40(7):910-922.

sessions.title: The humming breath
script: For this session, find a spot where a little noise won't bother anyone. We're going to hum together, with our mouths closed.
Sit down, with your back straight and relaxed. Let your shoulders drop, and your breath find its rhythm.
Breathe in through your nose… and breathe out calmly. Once more, letting your belly move freely.
You may have heard of the vagus nerve. It's become very fashionable in recent years, so let's untangle what's true from what's fuzzy.

The vagus nerve is one of the longest nerves in your body. It starts at the base of the brain, runs down through the neck, and branches out to the heart, the lungs, and a large part of the digestive system.
Its name comes from the Latin "vagus," meaning wanderer. It wanders through your whole torso.
A wandering nerve, if you like, that visits many of the places where you feel stress.

It's a major communication line that runs both ways. It carries messages from the brain to the organs. But it carries even more from the organs to the brain: how your stomach is doing, how fast your heart is beating, how your lungs are breathing.
It's part of the recovery system, the one that slows the heart and supports digestion and rest. It's a bit like your body's brake, against the accelerator of stress.
This brake is working all the time, even right now. You don't have to switch it on: you can simply give it a little more room.
A bit like your foot hovering near the brake pedal when you drive: it doesn't slam on the brakes, it keeps adjusting your speed.

Researchers track its activity through a measure called heart rate variability: the small, natural variations in time between heartbeats. A healthy heart isn't a metronome. It's constantly speeding up and slowing down, along with the breath.

So what seems to engage this brake? First, slow exhaling. When you breathe out, your heart slows slightly, and the vagus nerve plays a big part in that. Lengthening your out-breath means making use of a natural mechanism.
You can feel it for yourself some time: place two fingers on your wrist or your neck, and breathe slowly. For many people, the pulse speeds up a little on the in-breath, and slows on the out-breath.
Next, the voice. The vagus nerve also helps control the muscles of the throat and larynx, the ones that let you speak and sing.
And finally, a sense of safety. A familiar face, a gentle voice, a reassuring presence: all of these seem to help the body step out of alert mode.
Let's be honest: you'll sometimes read that you can "hack" your vagus nerve in a few minutes. The research doesn't go that far.
What we do know is that slow breathing helps many people feel calmer, and that humming is a very natural way to lengthen the out-breath.
A few studies, still small, also suggest that bee breath, a closed-mouth humming practice from yoga, may encourage relaxation. And many people simply enjoy the vibration it creates.
Humming has another advantage: it keeps the mind busy. It's hard to ruminate while you're making a sound and feeling its vibration.
Try worrying about tomorrow's meeting while you hum a long, low note. It's surprisingly hard.
It's a little like singing yourself a lullaby.
Let's try it.
One thing before we start: if your nose is blocked, or the sound bothers you, you can simply do the long out-breath, in silence.
Keep your mouth closed, your teeth slightly apart, your tongue resting. Your jaw is relaxed.
Close your eyes, if you like.
Start with a simple breath. Breathe in gently through your nose, then out through your nose, without doing anything special.
Once more. The air comes in, cool… and goes out, a little warmer.
Now we'll add the sound. On your next out-breath, hum a low, soft "mmm," like when you taste something delicious.
No need to sing in tune, or to be loud. The sound stays soft, almost inward. It happens only on the out-breath. The in-breath stays silent, through the nose.
Breathe in through your nose, letting your belly expand… and hum, for as long as it feels comfortable.
[pause 4s]
Very good. Let the sound finish in its own time, and breathe normally for a moment.
Notice the vibration it created. Maybe in your lips, your nose, your cheeks, or behind your eyes.
Notice, too, how the sound changed your out-breath: it becomes longer, steadier, almost effortless.
That longer out-breath is exactly what we were talking about a moment ago.
Once more. Breathe in through your nose, without filling your lungs all the way… and hum, letting the sound sink down into your throat and chest.
[pause 4s]
Place a hand on your chest, if you like, to feel the vibration under your fingers. Like a purr.
Notice your shoulders, too. They often soften on their own while you hum.
Your jaw stays soft, your teeth apart. Only your lips are gently closed.
Breathe in gently… and let the sound come, mmm.
[pause 4s]
You can try a slightly lower note, or a slightly higher one, to find the one that vibrates most pleasantly for you. Everyone has their own.
Breathe in through your nose… and hum your own note.
[pause 4s]
If you feel dizzy or short of breath, stop and breathe normally. Humming should stay easy, never forced.
Now let's slow down. With each round, let the sound last just a little longer, without straining. The in-breath stays simple and natural.

If you like, you can also gently close your ears with your index fingers, resting on the little flap of cartilage at the entrance of each ear. The sound becomes more inward, like listening to a seashell.
If it doesn't feel comfortable, simply keep your hands resting where they are.
Breathe in… and hum slowly, like a bee drifting away across a garden.
[pause 4s]
One last hum. Breathe in through your nose… and let the sound stretch out to the end of your breath, without going into discomfort.
[pause 4s]
Now let the sound fade away. Breathe naturally, through your nose, without controlling anything.
Stay for a moment in this calm. Notice what remains of the vibration, in your lips, your face, your chest. Like the echo of a bell fading away.
Your breath carries on by itself. There's nothing left to do, just listen to the quiet inside.
How is your breath now? Your heart? Your face? Your thoughts may be a little slower, more spaced out, like clouds drifting apart.

There's nothing in particular you should feel. Maybe relaxation, warmth, tingling. Maybe just silence. Everything is welcome. And if you didn't notice anything special, that's fine too: you've discovered a tool, and it gets easier with time.
Gently come back. Move your fingers, your shoulders. Open your eyes whenever you like.
As with any breathing practice, regularity is what counts. A few minutes a day will probably serve you better than one long session now and then.
You can take this humming anywhere a little sound is possible: in the shower, while cooking, before sleep. A few rounds are enough.
And where you can't make noise, at work or on the train, just keep the long, slow out-breath, as if you were humming on the inside. Your voice, even silent, is there to soothe you.
sources: Standard anatomy: vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) from brainstem to heart, lungs and much of the digestive tract; majority of fibres are afferent (organ-to-brain) - e.g. Berthoud HR & Neuhuber WL (2000), Auton Neurosci 85:1-17; Breit S et al. (2018), Front Psychiatry 9:44.
Vagal innervation of larynx/pharynx (recurrent and superior laryngeal nerves) - standard anatomy.

Respiratory sinus arrhythmia (heart slows on exhalation, vagally mediated): Yasuma F & Hayano J (2004). Chest 125:683-690; Gerritsen RJS & Band GPH (2018). Breath of life: the respiratory vagal stimulation model of contemplative activity. Front Hum Neurosci 12:397.

Bhramari (humming bee breath): small trials suggesting reduced heart rate / relaxation, e.g. Kuppusamy M et al. (2018) Sci Rep / review 'Effects of Bhramari Pranayama on health - a systematic review', J Tradit Complement Med 8(1):11-16. Evidence base is small - script says 'quelques études, encore petites'.
Script explicitly avoids polyvagal-theory claims and 'vagus hacking' promises; 'sentiment de sécurité' phrased with 'semble' (social safety and stress buffering: see Heinrichs et al. 2003).

HRV as index of vagal (parasympathetic) cardiac activity: Shaffer F & Ginsberg JP (2017). An overview of heart rate variability metrics and norms. Front Public Health 5:258; Laborde S, Mosley E & Thayer JF (2017). Front Psychol 8:213.

sessions.title: Your window of tolerance
script: Welcome. This session gives you a simple map for understanding your inner states, and two tools to find your way.
Sit with your feet on the floor. You can keep your eyes open the whole time: that's part of the practice.
Take a breath, at your own pace.
Feel the air coming in through your nose, and your back resting against the chair. You're simply arriving.
Clinicians, including the American psychiatrist Dan Siegel, have offered an image called the window of tolerance.
Picture a band, a zone, between two extremes. Inside this zone, you can feel emotions, even strong ones, while still being able to think. You can listen, choose, respond rather than react.
It isn't a state of perfect calm. Inside your window, there can be anger, worry, emotion, excitement. But you stay at the controls.
Think of a river flowing between two banks. The water can be calm or choppy, fast or slow. As long as it stays within its banks, it keeps on flowing.
Above the window is over-activation. Your heart pounds, your thoughts race. It's agitation, panic around the corner, anger taking over. Thinking clearly gets hard, and you react on a hair trigger.
Below it is under-activation. Here, it's more like emptiness. A sense of numbness, of being cut off from your feelings, flat. As if someone had dimmed the switch.
You might want to curl up under the covers, or scroll through your phone without really seeing anything.
Or you might stare at the same page for ten minutes without taking in a single word.
Both states are protective reactions of your nervous system. They're not flaws, and they're not failures.
Here's an example. You get an unpleasant email. Inside your window, you read it, feel the irritation rise, take a breath, and choose how to reply.
Above it, you fire back within a minute, hammering the keyboard, and regret it a little later. Below it, you shut the laptop and can't get anything done for the rest of the evening.
Nobody stays inside their window all the time. Leaving it is part of life. What matters is knowing how to come back.
The width of the window varies. Poor sleep, hunger, built-up stress can narrow it. Rest, connection with others, and practice can help widen it.
It's worth saying: this is a model, a map to help you find your bearings, not a precise measurement. But many people find it helps them understand themselves better.
Above all, it points the way. You don't return to your window the same way when you're too high as when you're too low. Too high, the aim is to come down. Too low, the aim is to come gently back up.
It's like a thermostat: when it's too hot, you don't turn up the heating. When it's too cold, you don't open the window.
Let's start by finding where you are.
Without changing anything, notice where you are right now.
Your energy, first. Is it rather high, jittery? Or rather low, heavy?
[pause 2s]
Your thoughts. Are they racing in every direction? Or slow, foggy, far away?
[pause 2s]
Your body. Is it tense, ready to spring? Or limp, heavy, hard to get moving?
[pause 3s]
Picture a vertical ladder, with your window in the middle. Where are you right now? A bit above, in the middle, a bit below?
Just a rough sense is enough. You don't need to be precise.
There's no right answer. Just information, which you can take in without judgment.
Sometimes you're a bit of both at once: exhausted and on edge. That's common. In that case, start with whichever tool feels most fitting.
And if you're not sure where you are, that's fine too. Just notice your energy right now, and let's move on.
Here's the first tool, for times when you're too high. Even if you feel fine right now, try it: practicing calm is how you remember it in the storm.
What helps when you're too high is anything that slows and grounds you: contact with the floor, the weight of your body, the out-breath.
Place both feet flat on the floor. Press them down a little, as if you wanted to leave a footprint.
Feel the weight of your legs. Imagine them growing heavy, anchored.
If you're sitting, feel the seat beneath you too, solid, carrying all your weight without any effort.
Now, the long out-breath. Breathe in through your nose, simply… two… three.
And breathe out slowly through your mouth, about twice as long as the in-breath, like a long, easy sigh… four… five… six.
[pause 3s]
Again. Breathe in through your nose… two… three… and blow out slowly, letting your shoulders drop… four… five… six.
[pause 3s]
One last time, and as the air leaves, think: "heavy and slow."
[pause 3s]
If you feel dizzy, simply go back to your natural breathing.
That's the first tool: heavy feet, long out-breath. It helps your body press the brake when everything speeds up.
You can use it anywhere: in a meeting, on the train, in a waiting room. No one even needs to notice.
Here's the second tool, for times when you feel switched off, empty, drained. Here, the aim isn't to calm down further. It's to gently wake up your senses.
What helps when you're too low is the opposite: anything that brings a little stimulation, movement, contact with your surroundings.
Keep your eyes open, and look around you. Let your gaze wander slowly across the room, from left to right.
Silently name three colors you can see.
[pause 3s]
Then find an object you hadn't noticed until now. Look at its shape, its texture.
Describe it silently, as if you had to explain it to someone who has never seen it.
You can also rest your hands on a cool surface, a table or a wall, and feel its temperature.
Now move a little. Rub your hands together briskly until you feel warmth. Then place them on your thighs, or on your face.
Stretch your arms up, or roll your shoulders. Always within what's comfortable, never into pain.
And now, a slightly livelier breath. Breathe in a little more fully through your nose, as if smelling something good, and breathe out naturally, without lingering.
Three or four breaths like that, at your own pace. No faster: we want to wake you up, not leave you breathless.
Breathe in with a little energy… and out. Again, in… and out. One last time, in… and out.
[pause 3s]
If you feel light-headed, slow down and breathe normally.
That's the second tool: look, move, breathe a little more fully. It helps your body come gently back up into its zone.
Now let's return to the center. Let your breathing find its own rhythm, neither too fast nor too slow.
Feel your feet on the floor, and at the same time, what's around you: the light, the sounds. Body present, mind available.
Pick out three sounds around you, near or far, while keeping your feet firmly planted.
Notice how, here, you can both feel your body and follow my voice. That's the window: feeling and thinking at the same time.
[pause 2s]
This is what your window feels like. Not necessarily deep calm. More a sense of being here, neither swept away by the storm, nor absent.
Take a few moments to savor it, and to remember it.
Notice the temperature of the air, the weight of your hands, the sounds in the room.
[pause 3s]
Over the coming days, I invite you to spot your own signals that you're leaving the zone.
Going up, it might be a rising voice, a clenching jaw, thoughts going round in circles.
Going down, maybe an urge to give up on everything, a blank stare, a sudden heaviness.
The earlier you recognize them, the easier it is to come back. Heavy feet and a long out-breath when you're too high. Look, move, breathe more fully when you're too low.

If you often find yourself outside your window, or go through periods where everything stays switched off for a long time, talking to a therapist or a doctor can really help. This isn't a path to walk without support.
For now, have a little stretch, and carry on with your day from the center of your window.
sources: Siegel DJ (1999). The Developing Mind. Guilford Press (origin of the 'window of tolerance' concept).
Ogden P, Minton K & Pain C (2006). Trauma and the Body: A Sensorimotor Approach to Psychotherapy. Norton (hyper-/hypo-arousal, regulation strategies).
Corrigan FM, Fisher JJ & Nutt DJ (2011). Autonomic dysregulation and the window of tolerance model of the effects of complex emotional trauma. J Psychopharmacol 25(1):17-25.
Yerkes RM & Dodson JD (1908) / inverted-U arousal-performance relationship (related idea).
Factors narrowing regulation capacity (sleep loss, hunger, cumulative stress): e.g. Walker MP & van der Helm E (2009) Psychol Bull 135:731-748 (sleep and emotional regulation).

Note: the window of tolerance is a clinical heuristic, not a measured construct - script says so explicitly. Orienting/movement/energising-breath tools are standard practice-based techniques, not claimed as proven.

sessions.title: Complete the stress cycle
script: Welcome. This session is a little more active than the others. At one point, I'll invite you to stand up and move. If that's not possible for you, you can do everything sitting down.
To begin, settle in however you like, and take a breath to arrive.
Breathe in through your nose… and out through your mouth, letting your shoulders drop.

Have you ever been through this? A hard week comes to an end. The project is handed in, the argument is settled, the exam is over. The problem is gone… and yet the tension is still there, in your shoulders, your stomach, your sleep.
Two American authors, Emily and Amelia Nagoski, offer a simple way to understand this gap. They separate the stressor from the stress.
The stressor is the cause: work, money, a conflict, an endless line at the store.
The stress is the reaction in your body: your heart speeding up, your muscles tensing, hormones circulating.
And here's the key idea: dealing with the stressor doesn't necessarily deal with the stress. You can solve the problem, and still carry the reaction in your body.
Think of a gazelle chased by a lion. If it escapes, it's because it ran with all its strength. Its body used up the energy that stress mobilized, then returned to calm. The cycle is complete.
We, on the other hand, face stressors we can neither run away from nor fight. We stay seated in front of a screen, heart pounding, jaw clenched. That mobilized energy has nowhere to go.
It's a bit like starting the car, revving the engine, and then sitting in neutral all day long.
And if these cycles stay open day after day, the tension builds up, a bit like a pile of dishes that never gets washed.
A sink full of dishes isn't a disaster on day one. After a few weeks, it becomes a real weight.

This is what these authors call an unfinished stress cycle. It's more of an image than a scientific theory in the strict sense. But it fits with well-established findings: physical activity, rest, slow breathing and social connection help the body return to calm.
So what tells your body the danger has passed?
Moving, first. It's one of the most effective ways: walking, dancing, running, anything that gets your body working.
Breathing slowly, with long out-breaths.
Laughing, really laughing, with someone. Not a polite little laugh: a real fit of giggles, the kind that shakes your belly.
Connection and affection: a warm conversation, a hug that lasts a little while, stroking a pet.
Creating, too: drawing, singing, writing down what you feel, playing music.
Anything that lets what's inside find a way out.
And sometimes, crying. Crying isn't failure. For many people, it's a way of releasing pressure.
Today, we'll complete the cycle together, in four steps: movement, breath, release, safety.
Before we start, notice how you feel on a scale from one to ten, where ten is maximum tension. Just keep that number in mind.
[pause 3s]
Step one: movement. If you can, stand up, and give yourself a little space. If not, stay seated and do the same movements with your arms and upper body.
An important reminder: never into pain. Always stay within what feels comfortable for you.
Start walking on the spot, gently. Lift one foot, then the other. Let your arms swing.
You can swing your arms a little more freely, as if you were walking briskly to catch a train. Feel your feet meeting the floor, one after the other.
Speed up a little, if it feels good. Lift your knees a bit higher. Feel your heart getting going, your breath deepening.
Your body is doing exactly what it was waiting for: using up this energy. For your body, it's a bit like finally escaping the lion.
Keep going a little longer. One, two, one, two. Let your arms follow the rhythm of your steps.
Now stop walking, and shake out your hands. As if you were flicking off drops of water.
Shake your arms, your shoulders. Let your whole upper body shake, loosely, like a dog coming out of the water.
You may have seen a dog shake like this after a fright, then trot off calmly. Here, it's simply a way to release the tension built up in your muscles.
Wrists loose, fingers relaxed. Shake, shake, as if you were shaking the day off your hands.
One leg, then the other. Shake them gently. And if you feel like making some noise, blowing out, sighing, go for it.
A few more seconds. Your whole body shaking. Letting out the energy that was stuck.
Five… four… three… two… one.
And stop. Stay still, standing or sitting. Feel what's moving through you: warmth, tingling, your heart beating.
[pause 3s]
Step two: the breath. As your heart slows down, we'll go along with it. Notice how, after effort, your breath naturally wants to lengthen.
Breathe in through your nose, for a count of four… two… three… four. And breathe out through your mouth, slowly… three… four… five… six… seven, like a long sigh.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Breathe in, feeling your belly rise… three… four. And breathe out, letting your body come back down, like a wave drawing back… five… six… seven.
[pause 3s]
Carry on at your own pace. With each out-breath, imagine telling your body: it's over, the danger has passed.
If you feel any dizziness, go back to your natural breathing.
One last slow breath. Breathe in… and breathe out, all the way, feeling your heart settle back into its easy rhythm.
Step three: release. If you were standing, sit down now, comfortably.
We'll tense and then release a few areas of the body. Tensing first often helps you feel the release more clearly. Keep breathing normally while you tense.
Make fists. Tight, but without hurting yourself. Hold the tension for a few seconds…
Three… two… one…
And let go. Let your hands open, and feel the difference.
[pause 3s]
Now lift your shoulders up toward your ears. Squeeze… hold…
Hold the tension… three… two… one…
And let them drop, all at once. Heavy.
Your legs, now. Press your heels into the floor, tighten your thighs… and let go.
Feel your legs growing heavy, as if after a long walk.
Scrunch up your whole face, as if you'd bitten into a very sour lemon. Eyes, nose, mouth.
And release. Your forehead smooths, your cheeks soften, your jaw falls slightly open.
[pause 3s]
Now let your whole body grow heavy in your seat. Arms, legs, back. Nothing to hold, nothing to do.
Your breath moves on its own. Your body is held by the seat beneath you.
[pause 3s]

Step four: safety. Place one hand on your heart and the other on your belly. Or both on your chest. You can also cross your arms and rest your hands on your shoulders, as if giving yourself a hug. Choose whatever you prefer.
Feel the warmth of your hands. The gentle movement of your breath under your palms.
Many people find this simple touch comforting. It's a gesture we make instinctively to console someone. Today, you're offering it to yourself.
You can say to yourself, silently: "I'm safe, here and now." Or: "It's over, I can rest."
Choose the words that feel true for you.
[pause 3s]
If those words don't feel true today, that's okay. Just keep the warmth of your hands, and the feeling of your breath.
Your body knows how to find its way back to calm. You're simply helping it find the path.
Now gently lower your hands, and notice how you feel.
Think back to the number you had in mind at the start, between one and ten. Where are you now?
[pause 3s]
Maybe the number has gone down. Maybe it's hardly moved, and that's useful information too. Sometimes built-up stress takes several cycles, several days, to unwind.
What you've just done, you can do again every day, in one form or another. What matters is choosing what suits you.

Maybe a brisk walk on your way home from work. Ten minutes of dancing in your kitchen. A fit of laughter with a friend. A long hug with someone you love. Or a few slow breaths, a hand on your heart, before you sleep.
Choose something that's realistic on a busy day, not just on a perfect one.
This isn't one more chore on your list. It's a way of telling your body, every day, that you're listening.
Think of one or two ways that feel like you, and that you could slip into your day, even briefly.
[pause 3s]
And if you feel that tiredness and tension have been settling in for a long time, despite everything, don't hesitate to talk to a doctor or a therapist. Exhaustion deserves to be taken seriously.
For now, take one last deep breath. You've given your body what it needed: the end of the story.
sources: Nagoski E & Nagoski A (2019). Burnout: The Secret to Unlocking the Stress Cycle. Ballantine (stressor vs stress; 'completing the stress cycle'; physical activity, breathing, positive social interaction, laughter, affection, crying, creative expression). Popular-science model - script says it is an image rather than a strict scientific theory.
Sapolsky RM (2004). Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers (prey animal escapes then returns to baseline).

Physical activity and stress reactivity/mood: e.g. Mücke M et al. (2018). Influence of regular physical activity and fitness on stress reactivity as measured with the Trier Social Stress Test protocol: a systematic review. Sports Med 48:2607-2622; Stults-Kolehmainen MA & Sinha R (2014) Sports Med 44:81-121.
Progressive muscle relaxation: Jacobson E (1938) Progressive Relaxation; McCallie MS, Blum CM & Hood CJ (2006). J Hum Behav Soc Environ 13(3):51-66.

Soothing touch/hand on heart: Dreisoerner A et al. (2021). Self-soothing touch and being hugged reduce cortisol responses to stress. Compr Psychoneuroendocrinol 8:100091 (single study - script only says many people find it comforting).
Crying as emotional release: Gračanin A, Bylsma LM & Vingerhoets AJJM (2014). Is crying a self-soothing behavior? Front Psychol 5:502 (mixed evidence - wording 'chez beaucoup de personnes').
Laughter and stress: e.g. Zander-Schellenberg T et al. (2020). Does laughing have a stress-buffering effect in daily life? An intensive longitudinal study. PLoS One 15(7):e0235851.
